title: Live Life Better
description: Fifteen Delhi-NCR schools learned food and responsible consumption, grew school food gardens and made one-minute films, with UNEP and the One Planet Network.
deck: What we buy, eat and throw away — taught for a year in fifteen Delhi-NCR schools, grown in fifteen school food gardens, and told back by the students in one-minute films.
identity: Swechha is an environmental organisation in Delhi, working since 2001 — air, the Yamuna, schools, journeys and a five-acre farm.
partnership: Supported by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) through the One Planet Network

what.head: The plate and the planet
what.lead: The project calls its subject sustainable consumption: where our food and our things come from, what they cost the planet, and what is left over when we are done with them. Young consumers make these choices every day and are taught the least about them.
what.line: Every lunchbox has a supply chain. Most students have never been asked to trace one.

rows.p: Consumer information. Sustainable lifestyles and low-carbon living. Food systems and zero waste. A plate of dal chawal is the way in to all three.

Fifteen schools across Delhi, Gurugram and Faridabad. Government schools have the ground for a garden and not the budget; private-school students have the consumption and the reach. The project needed both.

rows.h: Learn it, grow it, say it
rows.p: Workshops gave the knowledge. Gardens and compost put it in the students’ hands. A film festival gave them a way to tell everyone else.

rows.h: One part of a global strategy
rows.p: Live Life Better is part of the One Planet Network’s work to mobilise children and youth for the Global Strategy on Sustainable Consumption and Production, and SDG 12: responsible consumption and production.

kinds.head: Four deliverables
kinds.lead: Sixty workshops, fifteen gardens that had to last two seasons, compost where the canteen waste goes, and a film festival run by the students.

workshops.head: Workshops
workshops.lead: Four one-hour sessions in each of the fifteen schools, for students in classes five to nine, on food and responsible consumption — sixty in all, inside the school timetable.
prose: The first question was the easiest one to ask and the hardest to answer: did you have breakfast today, and do you know where it came from? Wheat takes four to five months to grow. One roti’s worth of it takes three to four hundred litres of water.

rows.p: Journey of Our Food. Seeds, Soil and Sustainability. Traditional Food Wisdom and Soil Composting. Responsible Consumption.
rows.cap: Each session is written out as a facilitator’s toolkit, with timings, materials and the films used in class.

rows.p: Games, short films, role-play and maps. Students trace each ingredient of a meal back to the state it grew in, work out its food miles, and use a carbon-footprint calculator built on Indian data.
The last sessions move from the classroom to the soil: seeds, compost and the bed the class will plant. The workshops are where the garden gets planned.

gardens.head: Food gardens
gardens.lead: Fifteen mini food gardens, one in each school, planted in the winter of 2025 — and replanted for the summer of 2026, which was in no plan.
prose: A garden planted once is a photograph. A garden planted twice is a habit. The summer replanting was the schools asking for a second season, and Swechha going back to give them one.

rows.p: Designed the beds, filled grow bags and drums, sowed seasonal vegetables and herbs, made compost and kept the garden watered. Soil health and urban farming, learnt with their hands.
Winter planting from October to December 2025. Summer replanting from July to September 2026, so every garden still works after the project ends.
Grow bags in a courtyard, raised beds by a boundary wall, a radish harvest in Gurugram. Each garden sits inside the school gate, and a class looks after it.

statement.line: Fifteen schools gave it a place in the year.

zero-waste.head: Towards zero-waste canteens
zero-waste.lead: The aim was a school cafeteria that sends nothing to landfill. No school got all the way there in a year, so students started the campaigns and the compost started taking the waste.
prose: A zero-waste canteen needs vendors, bins, space and a timetable to change at once. That is a school’s decision over years, not a project’s over months. A compost unit by the canteen door is where it starts.

rows.p: Awareness campaigns led by students, waste audits of what the canteen throws out, and compost bins and units installed in select schools to turn cafeteria waste into soil for the garden.
Space, infrastructure and contracts with canteen vendors. Fully zero-waste cafeterias need longer timelines and support from the school itself.
The compost feeds the food garden. Leftovers become soil, soil grows food, and the class that did the audit sees both ends.

films.head: The One-Minute Film Festival
films.lead: Students from the partner schools made films of sixty seconds or less on sustainable lifestyles and responsible consumption. A jury reviewed every entry, and the shortlisted films were screened.
prose: A workshop reaches a classroom. A one-minute film made by someone in that classroom reaches their friends, their family and everyone who follows them.

rows.p: Thinking before you buy. Low-carbon living. From farm to plate. Zero waste. One climate action a student, a family or a school has taken.
An expert jury of environmental experts, filmmakers and educators, looking for a clear message, a fresh way of telling it, and one thing a viewer can do.
Screened at the festival and shared through Swechha’s digital campaign on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, alongside the campaign’s own series on seasonal eating and food on our plates.

schools.head: The fifteen schools
schools.lead: Eleven government and municipal schools and four private schools, across Delhi, Gurugram and Faridabad. Each one took four workshops and kept a food garden.

rows.h: Hands in the soil keep the lesson
rows.p: Gardens and composting kept students engaged long after the workshop ended. What they planted, they came back to check on.
Campaigns started by students built more ownership than rules handed down to them. The canteen audits and the films were theirs.

rows.h: Systems take longer than a year
rows.p: A zero-waste canteen needs infrastructure and time that a school has to give it. The compost units are the first step the schools can now build on.
